The Joke That Is CJP

The Cockroach Janta Party, founded by Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) member Abhijeet Dipke, has compromised the sensitive personal information of people who were misled into believing that he was fighting for the cause of ‘students’ in the aftermath of the NEET paper leak.

For the unversed, Dipke had called upon his followers to register on his party’s website :
https://t.co/KlVSTjKcp6
soon after it was launched.

Later, the AAP member alleged that the government took down his website, a claim that was later found to be false. It has now come to light that the users who trusted Abhijeet Dipke with their personal information have now been left vulnerable at the hands of potential cybercriminals.

On Wednesday (1st July), OSINT expert Nisarga took to X (formerly Twitter) to expose vulnerabilities on the website of the Cockroach Janta Party.

Earlier in its brief existence, the site was live and then responded with standard HTTP 403 errors from Hostinger’s active servers before the hold took effect.

In domain management terms, “clientHold” is a standard EPP (Extensible Provisioning Protocol) status code controlled exclusively by the registrar, not by governments or external authorities. According to ICANN documentation and registrar policies, this status instructs the registry not to publish the domain in the DNS, effectively taking it offline until the registrar resolves the underlying issue. Such instruction can be issued only by the owner of the website, not third parties, not even governments. Alternately, the domain provider or the host can take the website offline due to various reasons.

It is commonly applied for routine administrative reasons such as incomplete WHOIS contact verification, billing or payment problems, compliance violations, or at the request of the domain owner. The clientHold affects resolution globally at the registry level, not at any country level.

On the other hand, when a government orders blocking a website, it is done through ISPs (Internet Service Providers) in the country, and the block only takes place in that country. In India, such a block is typically enforced through the Department of Telecommunications via ISP-level DNS poisoning, IP blacklisting, or URL filtering. Such actions allow the domain to still resolve correctly on international resolvers outside the country. That is why websites blocked by the Indian govt can be accessed in India through VPN.

Moreover, when one visits a website blocked by the govt, the browser displays a message saying the same. But when one visits cockroachjantaparty’s website, the browser displays the code DNS_PROBE_FINISHED_NXDOMAIN. This means the browser can’t find the domain because it has been deactivated.

Moreover, no public government orders, court directives, or official statements have been issued regarding https://t.co/n5u5L8JbZ5, further undermining the censorship claim.

Therefore, the analysis of the website shows that either it has been taken by Dipte himself, or the domain provider/host took it down due to some compliance issues. There is no evidence that the site was taken down on Indian government’s order.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Delhi ahead of the 10 October protest. The order remains unpublished, and the police communication conveying it is marked "Top Secret".

9 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the internet shutdown imposed in parts of Delhi ahead of the protest called for tomorrow, 10 October 2026, at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner. A communication dated 9 October 2026 from the Deputy Commissioner of Police, Special Cell (HQ), Delhi to the nodal officers of Airtel, Vodafone Idea, Jio and MTNL, shared by the news agency ANI, records that the Union Home Secretary has authorised, on the request of the Delhi Police, the suspension of "mobile internet services (all technologies)" within a radius of four kilometres of the Janpath-Kartavya Path crossing, from 10 pm on 9 October to 10 pm on 10 October 2026. It refers to order No. 22016/12/2019-CIS-IV dated 9 October 2026 and is marked "Top Secret" at the top and bottom of the page.

As per a media report by Live Law, the Solicitor General informed the Supreme Court today that the shutdown is confined to "certain sensitive pockets" and will be reviewed on the basis of security inputs. The communication describes a circle of about 50 square kilometres across the centre of the capital, which takes in Jantar Mantar, Connaught Place, India Gate, Parliament, the Supreme Court, the Delhi High Court, New Delhi Railway Station and hospitals including Ram Manohar Lohia and Lady Hardinge. This is about seven times the area of the suspension ordered around Jantar Mantar on 2 October, and it runs for twice as long.

Delhi Police has refused permission for the protest, and prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force in New Delhi district. Delhi Police asked for the gates of 57 metro stations to be closed from 9 pm today, and the Railways cancelled trains due at New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin between 4 am and 2 pm tomorrow. Hearing a challenge to these measures today, the Supreme Court directed that there be no complete prohibition on metro and train services and asked the authorities to keep in mind the principle of proportionality. As reported, that order did not examine the internet shutdown. We call for the order to be withdrawn, and for mobile internet to remain available across Delhi tomorrow.

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public knows the area and hours of this shutdown from a police communication marked "Top Secret" that was shared by ANI, and not from the government. That communication records no reasons, and the order of the Union Home Secretary to which it refers has not been made public. This is now a pattern and the order for the shutdown of 2 October around Jantar Mantar became public four days later, when the Hindu obtained a copy.

This secrecy is contrary to the law declared by the Supreme Court. In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Court held that "an order, particularly one that affects lives, liberty and property of people, must be made available". It directed the authorities to "publish all orders in force and any future orders" suspending telecom services, including the internet, "to enable the affected persons to challenge it before the High Court or appropriate forum". A democracy "sworn to transparency and accountability", the Court said, "necessarily mandates the production of orders as it is the right of an individual to know". The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, framed under Section 20 of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, now provide that every suspension order "shall be published", must state its reasons, and must be limited to a clearly defined geographical area and a specified duration. No order may be made unless the authority has considered that its objectives cannot be achieved by any other reasonable means.

The communication shared by ANI invokes Rule 3 of these Rules, the same Rule that requires the order to be published. It is nevertheless marked "Top Secret", the highest security classification used by the Government of India. In January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs issued orders bearing the same number to suspend the internet at Singhu, Ghazipur and Tikri during the farmers' protest, and those orders remain available on the Ministry's own website. An order cannot be published and kept "Top Secret" at the same time.

The government has placed no evidence before the public that a shutdown makes a protest safer. The available research is to the contrary as a 2019 study of shutdowns and protest in India by Jan Rydzak, then at Stanford's Global Digital Policy Incubator, found shutdowns "much more strongly associated with increases in violent collective action than with non-violent mobilization". The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights reported in 2022 that many shutdowns justified on grounds of public safety or national security "were followed by spikes in violence" (A/HRC/50/55). In December 2021, the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology recorded that neither the Department of Telecommunications nor the Ministry of Home Affairs had studied the impact of shutdowns.

A shutdown also prevents people from documenting and reporting what happens at a protest. The same UN report found that, “the inability to access tools to document and rapidly report abuses seems to contribute to further violence”. Without mobile internet, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A protester cannot upload a video as events unfold, and a person who is injured or detained cannot send a location to family or a lawyer. On 20 July 2026, mobile internet in Central Delhi was switched off amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters. In Manipur in 2023, video of an assault on two women on 4 May reached the public only on 19 July, while a shutdown imposed on 3 May was still in force. This is the impact an internet shutdown has which rather than preventing violence prevents the documentation of illegality.

Our demands:

We call upon the Ministry of Home Affairs and the Delhi Police to:
1) Withdraw order No. 22016/12/2019-CIS-IV dated 9 October 2026 and keep mobile internet services running across Delhi on 10 October 2026.
2) Publish that order, and every other suspension order issued in connection with the protest, forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.
3) Withdraw the "Top Secret" marking, and stop classifying suspension orders and the communications that convey them to telecom operators.
4) Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and publish its final order, as the Supreme Court required on 23 February 2024.
5) Ensure that journalists and members of the public can record and report from the protest sites without obstruction.

On October 2nd, the government blocked BitChat in India without making the order public. We only found out through a notice on the iOS App Store.

BitChat uses Bluetooth mesh technology to pass messages from phone to phone. During Jantar Mantar 1.0, when the internet was shut and blocking vans jammed even SMS, protesters used it to find each other and share water and medicines.

Calling it a national security threat makes little sense. It only works over short distances, and the block only stops new downloads. Anyone can install it across the border and come back. The only people affected are citizens exercising their right to peaceful assembly.

PROTEST
The words democracy and the right to protest are being used very often and very loosely, especially all over the media, social media and internet channels. People of India are highly offended about the constitutional right to protest being curtailed by the dictatorship and a state of emergency being imposed.
The very same people who are quick to use the words such as constitution and democracy have not even read the relevant provisions of the constitution permitting and governing the right to protest.
Only if you understand the four corners and conditions attached to the right to protest under the constitution can you fairly determine whether or not what is happening in our country with the CJP is permissible or not.
So here are the main propositions surrounding the right to protest under the constitution:
1. The right to protest is available only to citizens of India. Article 19 specifically starts with the qualifier that the rights therein are available to Indian citizens only. Hence a foreigner cannot participate in a protest in India whether directly by coming on to the Indian soil or indirectly by funding or inciting such protest from foreign soil as such foreign interference is prime facie detrimental to the sovereignty and integrity of the country.
2. The right to protest emanates from article 19(1)(b) of the constitution which provides that all citizens shall have the right to assemble peaceably and without arms. There is thus an inherent limitation enshrined in this provision itself and requires that every protest is peaceful and without arms. For a protest to be peaceful it cannot imbibe any form of violence in it. Violence as we know can take multiple forms, not only physical violence but also verbal violence, abuses, aggression, charging towards any person or property, and destruction of property are all acts which make an assembly of people non peaceful. In fact, a large crowd by itself is a source of overwhelming distress and concern to the residents of the community and the organizers of such crowd bear the onus to ensure it remains peaceful and under control.
3. Article 19(1)(b) is further circumscribed by article 19(3) which specifically overrides article 19(1)(b) and empowers the Government to make any law and implement reasonable restricting regulating such protests where it believes it is so in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India or in the interest of public order. There is thus a constitutional duty on the Government to ensure such peaceful assemblies remain peaceful and do not deteriorate to the point of spoiling public order at large.
Applying all of the above to the ongoing situation of protests by CJP the following emerge:
a. The right under 19(1)(b) is to assemble in a peaceful manner. As we have seen during the protests demanding resignation of the education minister or the protests taking place at this point of time demanding resignation of the CEC, there is widespread verbal assaults on the PM, the Government and the authorities, aggression towards the police force, vandalism and destruction of property. Rather than people sitting at one place in a peaceful manner as was done by Anna Hazare, these protests involve people marching aggressively from one place to another holding placards and hurling abuses. By no stretch of imagination this can be termed as a peaceful assembly.
b. For anyone to compare, the analogy can be whether they would be comfortable for their neighbors to assemble peacefully in the compound of their residence when such ‘peaceful assembly’ entails the neighbors holding placards and hurling abuses towards your family, your mother, your sister and shouting and disturbing the peace of the locality. If we cannot tolerate this being inflicted on us at our residence, it certainly cannot be allowed at a larger scale as is being done by CJP in the capital of the country.
c. For any assembly, the size of the crowd is a key determinant in whether or not it is peaceful. Take for instance you have 1 person standing on the road in front of your house, or 5 or 100…the level of threat and unease you will feel will be exponentially higher as the number grows. The convenors of the crowd would have the burden to ensure the crowd remains orderly and ‘peaceful’. Of course bigger the crowd, more easily the situation can deteriorate into a stampede, violence and aggression. Hence the form of assembly that can be termed peaceful is like that of a peaceful march which was undertaken by Gandhiji or the assembly by Anna Hazare at Jantar Mantar.
d. Foreigners are not considered eligible for such demonstrations. They cannot participate directly or indirectly in such assembly. Direct participation would be foreigners coming on to the Indian soil and participating in protests. By this definition Dhruv Rathee coming down to India to participate in the CJP protest is by no means constitutionally permissible and in fact tantamounts to direct interference in the affairs of the country by a foreigner. Indirect participation of foreigners in protest is also not allowed meaning thereby their funding protests true circuitous channels of finance rooted to parties in India is open to scrutiny as it would be a violation of the constitutional provisions. Thus, anybody who is protesting and invoking the right under 19(1)(b), such as the members of CJP, are obligated to disclose their source of funding to prove that such funding is not coming from foreign sources.
e. Protests cannot disturb public order. What is happening with the CJP protests is that there is wide scale disruption of routine of all other citizens whether by virtue of blockades that are having to be put up due to their marches and other disruptive forms of protest. There are other stoppages, traffic jams and shops are having to be closed thereby affecting the daily livelihood of ordinary citizens. By this benchmark also CJP protests are not within the ambit of the permitted peaceful assembly contemplated by the Constitution.
f. Action by the police force is within the ambit of the Constitution especially article 19(3) which empowers the Government to impose reasonable restrictions on peaceful assembly where they feel that this is affecting public order or the sovereignty or the integrity of India. Thus, simply demonizing the police by quoting words such as ‘democracy’, ‘constitution’ and ‘right to protest’ in vacuum is a fallacy and does injustice to the workers of the police force who are doing their job.
g. Lastly, it would serve the present Government and all future Governments well to dedicate certain venues out of the city away from central areas like Connaught Place for such protests thereby bringing a proper balance between the right to protest and the daily affairs and routine of the rest of the citizens of India. Let whoever wants to protest gather peacefully in such out of the way venues for as many days, weeks and months as they desire.
For anyone shouting hoarse about the breach of the constitutional right to protest of CJP members you need to read the constitution and the judgments surrounding article 19(1)(b). Regardless of the political party you support and regardless of the cause at hand, no provision of the Constitution supports or permits such wide scale disruption, abuses, aggression and vandalism as we are seeing at the hands of all these people who have taken to the streets in these protests.
It is not a fundamental right nor constitutionally permitted by any stretch of imagination as it does not amount to a peaceful assembly in any sense of the word ‘peaceful’.

Fine.

The company has already secured key regulatory approvals.

What remains involves spectrum allocation and security requirements.

That's a sovereign government asking a foreign satellite operator some very basic questions before allowing its network to operate across Indian territory.

A satellite network isn't just another consumer app.

It can become part of:

📡 Communications
🛰️ Critical infrastructure
🛡️ National security
🚨 Emergency response
⚔️ Military operations

And when the network is controlled by a private company headquartered outside India, questions about data, lawful access, network control, security auditing and continuity during a crisis aren't optional.

They're the whole point.

🎯 Strategic Lens

So yes, Elon.
Bring Starlink to India's villages.
Bring it to the mountains.
Bring it to the islands.
Bring connectivity to every Indian who needs it.
But do it on India's terms.

🇮🇳 Data stays under Indian jurisdiction.
🔐 Security audits happen under Indian rules.
⚖️ Indian law applies on Indian soil.
🛰️ And no switch in Texas decides what works over India during a national crisis.

That's sovereignty.

text:
DO NOT DO BUSINESS IN INDIA!

What exists is an Indian antitrust case in which the maximum penalty could be calculated on Apple’s global revenue, and Apple is fighting that formula in court.
India’s Competition Commission (CCI) has been investigating Apple’s App Store since 2021. Developers and groups including Match (Tinder), PhonePe and Paytm accused Apple of abusing a dominant position by forcing apps to use Apple’s in-app payment system and charging a commission of up to 30%. Apple denies the allegations. A final penalty order had still not been issued as of the latest reporting in September 2026; the Delhi High Court had barred the CCI from issuing one before 15 July 2026 while Apple’s challenge was pending.
The global-revenue issue comes from a 2023 amendment to the Competition Act and the CCI’s 2024 penalty guidelines. Those rules let the regulator fine a company up to 10% of its average global turnover from all products and services over the previous three financial years, not only India revenue or App Store revenue. Apple told the Delhi High Court that, applied to FY2022–FY2024, that cap would be about $38 billion. Its India revenue is far smaller — about $8.9 billion in FY25, against roughly $416 billion worldwide.
The CCI’s stated reason is deterrence. It argues that a fine based only on India sales would be too small to change the behavior of a global digital company, and that the global-turnover rule matches practice used in the EU. Apple calls the rule arbitrary, disproportionate and unconstitutional when the alleged conduct is limited to India, and has asked the court to strike it down. In May 2026 the CCI also shifted, at least for the investigation, to seeking Apple’s India-specific financials rather than global figures.

text:
Meta must stop silently withholding the Instagram accounts of independent journalists in India

13 October 2026

Since 9 October 2026, Instagram has made the accounts of several independent journalists covering the protests in Delhi unavailable in India. Utkarsh Gaur’s main account was withheld on 9 October, and Sunny Tomar’s soon after. On the night of 12 October, Instagram withheld the account of Shubhangi Das Gupta, a 22-year-old independent journalist, and her secondary account now appears to face the same action. Today, Journo Mirror’s account was withheld in India. Each received the same notice, that Instagram had, “temporarily restricted access to this account pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.” The notice does not say which authority made the demand, which rule was invoked, which post was objected to, or when the “temporary” restriction ends. It arrives as a no-reply notification after the account has gone dark, with no prior warning and no reason.

The same day, IANS and ANI, citing Delhi Police sources, reported that around 500 posts “spreading rumours or trying to create unrest among people” had been taken down. On 12 October, PTI had put the figure at 300, which means about 200 more in one day. The police have not said which posts were removed, from which platforms, under which provision, or whether anyone who posted them was told. We are also receiving reports of WhatsApp accounts being shut down and of mobile numbers being put through fresh KYC verification that leaves them unusable while it is pending. All of this comes alongside a timeline in which there was suspension of internet services and public transport in the heart of the national capital.

IFF condemns Meta’s withholding of entire journalist accounts on the strength of an unnamed “legal requirement”, and the Delhi Police’s practice of announcing a running censorship tally through anonymous sources. Meta must restore these accounts, tell every affected user who asked for the restriction and under what law, and stop turning demands about particular posts into the silencing of entire accounts.
The IT Rules, 2021, on which Meta’s notice relies, give it two routes to restrict content. The notice meets the conditions of neither. If Meta acted on a government demand, the route is Rule 3(1)(d). If Meta acted on its own, Rule 4(8) requires it, as a significant social media intermediary, to notify the user before disabling access, explain the grounds, and give an adequate opportunity to dispute the action. None of this happened. In this situation at present the entire burden will be shifted to the user to seek remedy under Rules 3(2) and 3A, where a user must first go to Meta’s Grievance Officer, who has 15 days, and then to the Grievance Appellate Committee, which has 30 more. In our experience these timelines are often not met, and a grievance against unnamed “legal requirements” is likely to be answered by pointing back to them. Whatever the intention, the effect is to keep a journalist off the platform for more than six weeks, exactly when her reporting matters most.

The Delhi Police figures raise their own questions. “Rumour” is not a ground for restricting speech under Article 19(2).  A count of 500 posts announced through unnamed sources does not let anyone tell whether a post was fabricated or simply showed something the police did not want seen. Nor is it obvious that 200 reasoned intimations, each signed by an officer of DIG rank and each identifying the provision, the unlawful act and the exact URL, were issued in a single day.

Our demands

1) Meta should restore every account withheld in connection with the protests where the underlying demand, if any, concerned specific posts, and restrict no more than the URLs named in a lawful reasoned intimation.
2) Meta should tell each affected user in writing which authority made the demand, the issuing officer’s rank, the provision relied on, the content identified, and when the restriction will end.
3) Meta should disclose whether its systems automatically extend demands about individual posts to entire accounts, and stop any such escalation immediately.
4) The Delhi Police should publish the takedown requests it has issued, with their number, platforms, provisions, issuing officers and reasons, as Anuradha Bhasin requires.
5) MeitY should ensure notice and a hearing to every person whose content is restricted, publish the outcome of the monthly Secretary-level review under Rule 3(1)(d), and stop using Section 79(3)(b), the Sahyog Portal and “temporary” restrictions under the IT Rules to bypass the safeguards of Section 69A.
If you have been affected

If your post or account was withheld or removed in connection with the protests, or you received a notice about a police data request, write to legal@internetfreedom.in for pro bono assistance. Keep screenshots of every notice, note the date and time, and delete nothing. Document, document, document.

text:
I have my twitter back. 

It took me 6 days, a cyber police complaint and a legal notice to twitter to recover my account. 

If you got a DM from me last week asking you to vote for me for a podcast, that was not me. Please don't click it & If you already did, please change your password ASAP.

Here's what happened:

→I received a late night DM from a friend to vote on a podcast which redirected me to a a login page that looked right, and I typed in my password (classic)

→The attacker logged in and changed my 2FA within minutes & I was locked out of my account. (I still don't understand how my email and phone number were changed. Neither my email nor my phone was compromised.)

→Then he used account to DM followers a fake "vote for me" link. Each person who clicks becomes the next account sending it. That is how these spread.

What didn't work:

→ I filed X's hacked account form within the hour. Less than two hours later, the reply came: X could not verify me as the account owner. Their suggestion was to create a new account. Once 2FA is changed, the automated system treats the attacker as the real owner.

→ So I went to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, 2021, X must appoint a Resident Grievance Officer in India. He has no email address. X does not accept legal notices by email. 

The only options are a web form or post to their physical office.

Here's what worked:

→First, a cyber complaint on https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW (or call 1930).

→Second, a legal notice to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, impersonation complaints must be acted on within 24 hours.

→Third, the same notice sent by registered post, and to every X email address I could find.

The notice put X on record. It set out the ticket number, the phishing link, and the cyber complaint number. It showed proof of ownership: the registered email, the phone number, and the Premium subscription paid from my card. It ended with a clear ask and a deadline.

Six days after the hack, I was back in.

If this happens to you:
• Act within hours
• File X's hacked account form from your registered email and be persistent (this is important)
• File at https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW and keep the acknowledgement
• Notice to the Grievance Officer via the https://t.co/YkDfcMQwzE form and by post

Celebrating RTI Act on 12th October : Objective incomplete without Citizen’s Charter and Grievance Redressal Bill

There was a proposal to introduce “The Right of Citizens for Time Bound Delivery of Goods and Services and Redressal of their Grievances Bill, 2011” (The Citizen’s Charter and Grievance Redressal Bill) after implementation of “Right-To-Information Act, 2005” to fulfill the objective of providing timely redressal of Grievances to the public. But unfortunately the much-awaited and most desired bill has still not been introduced. Rather “The Citizen’s Charter and Grievance Redressal Bill” is much more necessary to achieve the desired goal. Union Government should fulfill the much-needed requirement by introducing the said bill which will make government-functionaries to solve problems of the people in an effective manner reducing over-burdened government-functionaries presently utilizing much of their time and resources Under Right-To-Information Act. Rather with quick disposal of public-grievances through “The Citizen’s Charter and Grievance Redressal Bill” will make government-functionaries working fast thus resulting in further savings of time and resources of government-departments and public authorities.

Otherwise also, a fresh look is necessary for revising RTI Rules drafted long back in the year 2012 to prevent misuse of RTI Act which will further drastically reduced time and resources of public authority spent on handling RTI matters. Ever since first amendment in RTI Act was done ever since its implementation on 12th October2005, some NGOs and opposition parties are crying that sunshine Act is diluted! But the amendment made in the year 2019 aimed to change status and tenure of Information Commissioners, in no way affected users of RTI Act. Insertion of section 44(3) in “The Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023” removing riders to section 8(1)(j) of RTI Act in fact necessary to preserve Parliamentary privilege and remove confusion through the term “public-interest”. Having a rider of “Public Interest” was not needed in view of section 8(2) of RTI Act which provides access to information in case public interest overweighs the harm protected. It is for the first time that Central Information Commission has full strength of Chief Information Commissioner and ten Information Commissioners sworn on 15.12.2025.

Otherwise also, earlier two Commissioners went on disposing the cases at a fast speed with Vinod Kumar Tiwari having disposed of 12700 cases with quality judgements elaborately worded in a short span of just 24 months while this figure does not include matters of Show-Cause notices and Non-Compliance matters. It is significant that he even heard some cases on different dates to ensure enough opportunity to respondent public-authorities to defend their case like in his verdict dated 16.01.2025 in petition-number CIC/GNCTD/A/2024/108412 in the matter “Sanjeev Kumar versus Directorate of Health Services (GNCTD”. He even imposed penalty on the PIO and awarded compensation to the petitioner apart from making recommendations while highlighting malpractices in working of private hospitals with DHS being the mute spectator.  Even Delhi High Court dismissed a writ-petition WPC 596/2026 against this verdict on first day of hearing i.e. 16.01.2026. Even present Chief Information Commissioner Raj Kumar Goyal echoed likewise in his verdict dated 16.01.2026 observing that despite 20 years of implementation of the RTI Act, public information officers and first appellate authorities in DHS (GNCTD) were not alert to their legal responsibilities terming it to be a serious issue.

At the same time, Vinod Kumar Tiwari praised such officers who respond to matters nicely not only while responding to RTI applications, but also while presenting their case before the Commission. Example is decision dated 17.11.2025 in file-number CIC/DDATY/A/2024/114518 in the matter “Pawan Jindal versus Delhi Development Authority (DDA)” where he praised Rahul Gupta, PIO-cum-Executive Engineer (DDA) for his nicely presenting the case before the Commission.  Such praise in a CIC-verdict motivates others to do similar nice work to handle RTI matters.

However, RTI rules (and not the RTI Act) need important modifications mainly to prevent misuse of the Act and minimising challenge to CIC verdicts in courts. Notification should be to declare all public-private-partnerships, sports-bodies, cooperative-societies and other such bodies, public-authorities under RTI Act. Land and Building Departments of central and state governments should study all cases of allotment of land or government-accommodations at subsidised rates or lease, and declare all these as public-authorities under RTI Act. For future, land or government-accommodations should be provided at subsidised rates on pre-condition of beneficiaries coming under purview of RTI Act.

Offices like those of President, Prime Minister, Governor, Lt Governor and Chief Minister must not act like “Post Offices” by transferring RTI applications under section 6(3) of RTI Act to concerned departments. These offices should entertain RTI applications pertaining to their respective offices only, and returning rest others to RTI applicants advising applicants to file RTI applications directly to concerned departments.

Considering vast participation of public-money in private sector banks, all private sector banks must be under purview of RTI Act. Already all employees up-to highest post of CMD are public servants according to Banking Regulation Act. Reserve Bank of India (RBI) had to impose restrictions on withdrawal of money for some time on a prominent private sector bank. Former CMD of another prominent private sector Bank is under arrest for serious charges of misappropriation of public-money in the Bank. Inspection Reports of private banks revealed under RTI Act by RBI reveal gross misuse of public money by top management. Another private sector bank is in notoriety for large number of Non-Performing Assets (NPAs). Heavy fluctuation in share-prices of certain private sector banks tend to doubt regarding safety of public money in private sector banks. Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (RBI subsidiary) has to pay maximum rupees five lakhs from state-funds to each depositor of the bank including those in private sector which collapses due to massive irregularities, which is public-funding to declare private sector banks as “public-authorities” under section 2(h) of RTI Act.

Section 27 and 28 of RTI Act give power to Competent Authorities and state-governments to draft their own rules which include fixing of RTI fees. Several Competent Authorities and states misused their power by having RTI fees as high as rupees 500However Supreme Court in its verdict dated 20.03.2018 imposed a capping of rupees fifty to be maximum RTI fees. RTI-fees should be uniformly rupees 50 inclusive of copying-charges of first twenty copied pages Making basic RTI-fees at rupees fifty will largely prevent misuse of RTI Act. There must not be any fees for filing First or Second Appeals.

Handling cost of a postal-order of value rupees ten costs postal-department about rupees fifty with cost of handling of postal-orders by a public-authority and bank-clearing even extra. Postal Department should issue special RTI-stamps (like earlier stamps for licence-fees of radios and TV sets) in denominations of rupees 2, 10 and 50 which will save crores of rupees annually to public-exchequers in using postal-orders as mode of payment of RTI fees.  These RTI stamps should be available at all post-offices and counters of public-authorities and other convenient sale-points. Post-free RTI-applications addressed to central public-authorities should be accepted at all about 160000 post-offices rather than just about 4500 post offices presently. It is not difficult because every post-office however small it may be, daily sends post-bag to Head Post Office with registered post, cash and unsold revenue-articles. This post-bag can carry post-free RTI-applications received at the post-office.

Decision dated 02.11.2012 by Punjab & Haryana High Court in the matter “Fruit and Vegetable Union versus Unknown” (CWP 4787 of 2011) requiring ID proof compulsorily with every RTI application, First Appeal and petitions filed with Information Commissions should be compulsorily adopted throughout the country Police-enquiry conducted at behest of some Indian missions abroad established that a petitioner approached Central Information Commission with name and address both of which did not exist. RTI-responses and orders of First Appellate Authorities should be auto-emailed rather than RTI-applicants required to search portals for viewing of RTI-responses and orders by First Appellate Authorities. Websites designed by National Informatics Centre (NIC) for central public-authorities should be mandatorily for all states. This has become necessary for state like Odisha which has made online filing of RTI-applications a mockery when it is compulsory to download online-filled RTI-application, and then send it by post to concerned department.

Delhi High Court in its order dated 08.08.2018 in WPC 8278 of 2018 in the matter “Anil Dutt Sharma versus Government of NCT Delhi and others” mentioned – This Court is of the prima facie view that the Right-To-Information Act, 2005 would now override the Delhi Right To Information Act, 2001. DRTI Act has lost all with implementation of RTI Act 2005. Very few applications are filed under DRTI Act. All such acts legislated by individual states, before RTI Act 2005 came into existence must be repealed.

text:
Hey everyone, have you been keeping up with this massive development in the Sambhal Masjid survey case? The Supreme Court has just made a ruling that's setting the stage for some real legal fireworks. Let's break this down because it's not just legal mumbo jumbo; it's a significant moment for cultural heritage, religious rights, and historical truth.

What Just Happened?

The Supreme Court, through a bench led by CJI Sanjiv Khanna and Justice Sanjay Kumar, has allowed the Advocate Commissioner to submit the survey report on the Sambhal Mosque to the trial court, but in a sealed cover. This is a big deal because:

1. No Stay Order: The SC didn't put a stay on the trial court's order to survey the mosque. This means the process isn't halted; it's just moving forward under wraps.

2. Masjid Committee's Next Move: The court has directed the Masjid Committee to approach the High Court, indicating that the legal battle is far from over. This gives the committee a chance to contest the survey's implications at a higher judicial level.

3. Sealed Cover Submission: The report will be given in a sealed cover. This is often done in sensitive cases to ensure that the court is the first to review potentially contentious information, maintaining judicial integrity.

Why This Matters:

- Places of Worship Act, 1991: This act was meant to preserve the religious character of places as they existed on August 15, 1947. However, it doesn't apply to monuments protected by the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), like the Jama Masjid in Sambhal. This exception is crucial because it opens the door for legal scrutiny that wouldn't be possible under the Act's general protection.

- The Purpose of the Survey: The original case, filed by Advocate Vishnu Shankar Jain, aimed to determine the mosque's character. Now, with the survey report being submitted, it's about getting closer to answering this question. 

- Legal Implications: The Hindu side isn't viewing this as a victory for the Masjid side because the report's submission means the investigation into the mosque's origins and character will continue. The sealed cover ensures that the findings are preserved for judicial review before any public or media speculation.

What's Next?

- Trial Court's Role:*The trial court has a scheduled hearing on January 8. There's no rush to proceed until the Masjid Committee makes its move in the High Court, which could potentially challenge or affirm the survey.

- High Court's Potential Decision: Depending on how the Masjid Committee argues their case, the High Court could either validate the survey's continuation or find grounds to halt or alter the process.

The Broader Conversation:

This isn't just about a piece of land or a structure; it's about history, identity, and legal rights:

- Cultural Heritage: Every stone, every inscription, every architectural feature of a site like this could tell a story of a civilization. If there's evidence suggesting a different historical use of the site, that's a story that needs to be told, preserved, and understood.

- Religious Rights: The sanctity of places of worship is a sensitive topic. For communities, these are not just buildings but embodiments of faith. How do you balance the right to worship with the right to investigate historical claims?

- Legal Precedents: This case could set a precedent for how religious disputes over historical sites are handled in India, especially where ASI protection plays a role. It's a test of how the legal system can navigate through claims of history, archaeology, and religious sentiment.

- Political Undercurrents: Let's not ignore that such cases often have political dimensions. They can influence community relations, electoral politics, and even national security concerns.

Reflections:

- Transparency and Justice: The sealed cover ensures that the findings aren't tampered with or sensationalized before judicial review, promoting a form of transparency where justice is seen to be done by the court first.

- Community Dialogue: This is an opportunity for dialogue between communities. If handled with sensitivity, it could lead to a mutual understanding of history and coexistence.

- Educational Value: Whatever the outcome, this case is a lesson in how history, law, and religion can intersect in modern contexts, offering insights into how societies deal with their past.

While the Supreme Court's decision might seem procedural, it's a pivotal moment in a case that touches on deep historical, cultural, and religious issues. It's a moment for all of us to watch, learn from, and reflect upon. Let's hope that justice, in its truest form, prevails, ensuring that historical truths are respected alongside the rights and sentiments of all involved communities. Keep an eye on this space; it's more than just legal news; it's a narrative of our shared heritage.

Department drags Assessee into time-barred demands and parallel ITC proceedings; High Court steps in to quash the demand order.

Issue :
The primary controversy was whether the Demand-cum-Show Cause Notice issued under Section 74(1) for the financial year 2017-18 was hopelessly barred by the statutory period of limitation prescribed under Section 74(10) of the CGST Act. The companion controversy was whether central tax authorities retained jurisdiction to initiate proceedings concerning excess Input Tax Credit for the financial years 2018-19 and 2019-20 when state tax authorities had already initiated and dropped proceedings on the identical subject matter, attracting the statutory bar under Section 6(2)(b) of the CGST Act.

Rule:
Section 74(10) of the CGST Act mandates that any adjudication order must be passed within a strict outer limit of five years from the statutory due date for furnishing the annual return, and administrative extensions granting taxpayers extra time to file returns do not automatically stretch the Department's period of limitation. Under Section 6(2)(b) of the CGST Act, as settled by the Supreme Court in M/s Armour Security (India) Ltd., where one tax administration has formally commenced adjudicatory proceedings by issuing a show cause notice on a specific tax liability, the other tax administration is strictly prohibited from initiating parallel proceedings on the same subject matter. Furthermore, the exceptional five-year window under Section 74(1) strictly requires explicit jurisdictional preconditions of fraud, wilful misstatement, or suppression of facts to evade tax, none of which can be assumed from routine investigative scrutiny or audit letters.

Application:
Regarding the financial year 2017-18, the statutory due date for filing the annual return was 31.12.2018, which meant the five-year limitation period available to the Department conclusively expired on 31.12.2023. The Department issued the impugned show cause notice only on 22.07.2024. Notification No. 06/2020 issued under Section 168A was purely intended to mitigate taxpayer hardship by extending return-filing dates and did not enlarge the Department's statutory limitation to initiate recovery. Moreover, an earlier inquiry letter dated 22.03.2021 was merely an administrative probe regarding VAT deposits rather than an adjudicatory notice alleging fraud or suppression. Regarding the financial years 2018-19 and 2019-20, state authorities had already issued show cause notices for mismatches between credit ledger entries and annual returns before dropping those proceedings. The central authority’s subsequent notice covering the identical excess credit issue violated Section 6(2)(b) because it sought to re-adjudicate an identical infraction. Conversely, allegations regarding short payment of tax for those years and return mismatches for the financial year 2020-21 were distinct causes of action and remained legally permissible.

Conclusion:
The High Court held that the proceedings for the financial year 2017-18 were completely barred by limitation and that the proceedings concerning excess Input Tax Credit for the financial years 2018-19 and 2019-20 were hit by the bar against parallel proceedings under Section 6(2)(b). Consequently, the High Court partly quashed the show cause notice to the extent of these jurisdictional defects, set aside the Order-in-Original in its entirety, and remitted the matter back to the Joint Commissioner for fresh adjudication strictly confined to the surviving issues within three months, reserving full liberty to the Assessee to contest the invocation of Section 74 on merits.

Impact Analysis:
This ruling protects taxpayers from dual scrutiny by preventing Centre and State authorities from reopening identical credit mismatches while making it clear that the Department cannot stretch statutory limitation periods using routine return-filing extension notifications.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s statement on wrongful content takedown by social media platforms 

Earlier today, @Meta temporarily removed Prime Minister Narendra Modi's video on the NEET paper leaks in India. According to media reports, a Meta spokesperson stated that the post was taken down due to an error and it had since been restored, post-haste.

The temporary removal of PM Modi's post highlights the larger issue of wrongful content takedowns by these platforms, often without any notice to users and leaving them with no meaningful recourse. These takedowns may be carried out by automated systems that have  been deployed as part of the growing due diligence obligations under Rule 3 of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, or by way of government-issued order which reflects as a “legal request” on the platform.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has seen multiple instances of automated monitoring systems wrongfully taking down content, with no available recourse but engaging with the platform's internal appeals mechanisms and grievance officers. While high profile instances such as this are resolved quickly, ordinary users are often left high and dry. These issues are exacerbated by the lack of human review in the escalation process, with aggrieved users facing constant automated and AI generated responses which often fail to address even the most apparent errors in moderation. Coupled with unresponsive and inefficient grievance officer reporting procedures, users are all but helpless. Platforms may deploy these automated systems to deal with the huge volumes of content that they have to moderate under the existing regulatory system, especially since many of these obligations are tied to the safe harbour provisions under the IT Act that exempt platforms from being liable for the content they host. However, having humans in the loop for grievance redressal would ensure that fair outcomes are delivered to all and not only to high-profile persons.

According to media reports, the Delhi Police has also identified around 450 social media accounts that allegedly shared deepfakes and AI generated content related to the protests. The Delhi Police has directed social media platforms to remove this kind of content shared during the CJP protests, along with other content considered "objectionable" that relates to the Prime Minister.

Such vague orders that invoke generic grounds such as “objectionable” or “offensive” are inconsistent with the safeguards laid down in Shreya Singhal. The Supreme Court upheld Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 strictly because it required that blocking orders must be reasoned, necessary, and proportionate, and that such reasons must be recorded in writing to enable judicial review. In the present case, notices sent to social media intermediaries through the Sahyog Portal under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act and Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, leave users in the dark, with no recourse to meaningfully challenge takedowns and leave affected parties without legal redressal. The Sahyog Portal puts in place a parallel system to take down content online, without any of the safeguards present under Section 69A.

The opacity surrounding the reasons for these takedowns goes against the strict requirements of accountability and record-keeping embedded in the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009. Instead, what we see emerging through these takedowns is a system of informal, decentralised censorship, where various government and law enforcement bodies decide the limits of free speech without transparency or oversight. An illustrative example is the temporary restriction faced by the @Cockroachisback’s primary Instagram handle, which was entirely blocked  on the evening of July 22. As per media reports, the account was restored after the Union Government reversed the blocking and advised the law enforcement agency that “action should be limited to specific posts or URLs instead of the entire account.”

It is not just the Prime Minister’s  post or CJP’s account that has faced such removals recently. Under the decentralised and opaque content removal regime, dozens of Instagram posts and videos related to the protests have been taken down, either by automated systems or in response to government orders, and many users have even had their accounts restricted. For these users, without high-profile attention, regaining access to their accounts or having the content restored is a long and arduous process, with no guarantee of remedy or reprieve.

Order -

“Meta is directed to remove, disable access to, and permanently take down the impugned content identified by the plaintiff from platforms operated by them, including but not limited to videos, reels, posts, accounts.”

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.
